chapter: Ch 4 — Price Determination in Different Markets

questions.stem: In economics, the term 'market' means:

options.text: any arrangement or contact between buyers and sellers of a good to fix a price and trade
options.explanation: Correct. A market is not a place but an arrangement through which buyers and sellers are in touch to fix a price and trade, wherever they are located.

options.text: a fixed physical place where goods are displayed for sale
options.explanation: A physical marketplace is only one example. Buyers and sellers trading through a screen across cities form a market with no common place.

options.text: the total stock of a good held by all sellers
options.explanation: That is supply, not the market. A market is the contact between the two sides, buyers and sellers.

options.text: the government body that regulates trade
options.explanation: A regulator is not the market. The market is the arrangement through which buyers and sellers themselves fix a price.

questions.sourceRef: Market = arrangement/contact between buyers and sellers, not a place

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Markets · One market one price
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the essentials of a market in the economic sense?

options.text: A commodity or service to be traded
options.explanation: This is an essential: a market must have something being bought and sold.

options.text: Buyers and sellers in contact with one another
options.explanation: This is an essential: a market is precisely the contact between the two sides.

options.text: A tendency toward one price for the good
options.explanation: This is an essential: competition pushes the good toward a single ruling price across the market.

options.text: A single fixed building where trade must occur
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed building is NOT essential; buyers and sellers can trade across distance, so no common location is required.

questions.sourceRef: Essentials: commodity, buyers and sellers in contact, one price; no fixed place

questions.stem: On the basis of TIME, markets are classified into:

options.text: local, regional and international markets
options.explanation: This is classification by area (geographical extent), not by time.

options.text: very short period, short period and long period markets
options.explanation: Correct. Marshall's time classification is the market (very short) period, the short period and the long period, by how far supply can adjust.

options.text: perfect, monopoly and oligopoly markets
options.explanation: This is classification by competition (market structure), not by time.

options.text: wholesale and retail markets
options.explanation: This distinguishes the stage of trade, not the time element used by Marshall.

questions.sourceRef: Time classification: market/very short, short and long period

questions.stem: A defining feature of a perfectly competitive market is:

options.text: a single seller of the product
options.explanation: A single seller is monopoly. Perfect competition has a very large number of sellers.

options.text: a very large number of sellers of a homogeneous product
options.explanation: Correct. Perfect competition has very many sellers, an identical (homogeneous) product and free entry, so each firm is a price taker.

options.text: a differentiated product with heavy advertising
options.explanation: Product differentiation and selling costs mark monopolistic competition, not perfect competition.

options.text: a few interdependent sellers
options.explanation: A few interdependent sellers is oligopoly. Perfect competition has too many sellers for any interdependence.

questions.sourceRef: Perfect competition: many sellers, homogeneous product, free entry

questions.stem: Under monopoly:

options.text: there is a single seller with no close substitute and blocked entry
options.explanation: Correct. A monopoly has one seller of a product with no close substitute, and entry is blocked, so the firm is the whole industry and a price maker.

options.text: there are many sellers of an identical product
options.explanation: Many sellers of an identical product is perfect competition, not monopoly.

options.text: the firm is a price taker
options.explanation: A monopolist is a price maker, not a price taker; it sets the price along the demand curve.

options.text: entry of new firms is completely free
options.explanation: Free entry is a feature of competitive markets. Monopoly rests on blocked entry, which lets profit persist.

questions.sourceRef: Monopoly: single seller, no close substitute, blocked entry, price maker

questions.stem: The distinguishing feature of monopolistic competition, compared with perfect competition, is:

options.text: a single seller
options.explanation: A single seller is monopoly. Monopolistic competition has many sellers.

options.text: an identical, homogeneous product
options.explanation: An identical product is perfect competition. Monopolistic competition is marked by a differentiated product.

options.text: product differentiation among many sellers
options.explanation: Correct. Monopolistic competition keeps many sellers and free entry but each sells a differentiated product, giving it some price control.

options.text: blocked entry of new firms
options.explanation: Entry is free under monopolistic competition. Blocked entry belongs to monopoly.

questions.sourceRef: Monopolistic competition: many sellers, differentiated product, free entry

questions.stem: The defining feature of an oligopoly market is:

options.text: a very large number of small sellers
options.explanation: Very many small sellers is perfect or monopolistic competition. Oligopoly has only a few sellers.

options.text: a few sellers whose decisions are interdependent
options.explanation: Correct. Oligopoly has a few sellers, each large enough that its price and output decisions affect the others, so the firms are interdependent.

options.text: one seller with no rival
options.explanation: One seller with no rival is monopoly. Oligopoly has several rival firms watching one another.

options.text: completely free entry with no barriers
options.explanation: Oligopoly usually has barriers to entry. Completely free entry describes the competitive forms.

questions.sourceRef: Oligopoly: few sellers, interdependence, barriers to entry

questions.stem: The term 'imperfect competition' refers together to:

options.text: perfect competition and monopoly
options.explanation: These are the two theoretical extremes, not the imperfect forms in between.

options.text: monopolistic competition and oligopoly
options.explanation: Correct. The two market forms between the extremes — monopolistic competition and oligopoly — are together called imperfect competition.

options.text: monopoly and oligopoly only
options.explanation: Monopoly is a pure extreme, not part of imperfect competition. The imperfect forms are monopolistic competition and oligopoly.

options.text: a single fifth market form of its own
options.explanation: Imperfect competition is not a separate fifth form; it is the umbrella name for the middle two forms.

questions.sourceRef: Imperfect competition = monopolistic competition + oligopoly

questions.stem: An 'industry' in economics means:

options.text: a single producing unit or factory
options.explanation: A single producing unit is a firm, not an industry.

options.text: the group of all firms producing the same or a closely similar good
options.explanation: Correct. An industry is all the firms making the same or a closely similar product; one such firm is a firm.

options.text: the government department for manufacturing
options.explanation: An industry is the group of producing firms, not a government department.

options.text: the buyers of a particular good
options.explanation: Buyers form the demand side. An industry is the group of producing firms on the supply side.

readLink.label: Read: Firm, industry and the time element, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Firm = one producing unit; industry = all firms making the same good

questions.stem: In Marshall's 'very short (market) period', the price of a good is determined mainly by:

options.text: demand, because supply is fixed
options.explanation: Correct. In the market period output cannot be changed, so supply is fixed and demand is the dominant force fixing the price.

options.text: the cost of production alone
options.explanation: Cost of production dominates in the long period, when supply can fully adjust — not in the fixed-supply market period.

options.text: supply, because output can be freely increased
options.explanation: Output cannot be increased in the market period; supply is fixed, so it is demand, not supply, that rules the price.

options.text: government price control
options.explanation: The market period result is about demand meeting a fixed stock, not about administered prices.

readLink.label: Read: Firm, industry and the time element, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Market period: supply fixed, demand dominant in price setting

questions.stem: In the long period, price is governed mainly by the conditions of supply because:

options.text: demand disappears in the long run
options.explanation: Demand does not disappear; it still matters, but supply becomes fully adjustable, so cost of production dominates.

options.text: all factors of production are variable and supply can fully adjust
options.explanation: Correct. In the long period all factors vary and firms can enter or leave, so supply is fully responsive and cost of production governs price.

options.text: output is completely fixed
options.explanation: Fixed output describes the market period. In the long period output is fully variable.

options.text: only variable factors can be changed
options.explanation: Changing only variable factors is the short period. In the long period all factors, including plant, can change.

readLink.label: Read: Firm, industry and the time element, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Long period: all factors variable, supply/cost of production dominant

questions.stem: Fresh vegetables are usually sold in a:

options.text: local market
options.explanation: Correct. Perishable and bulky goods such as fresh vegetables are sold near where they are produced, in a local market.

options.text: international market
options.explanation: International markets suit durable, high-value goods like gold or oil, not perishable vegetables sold nearby.

options.text: national market only
options.explanation: Fresh vegetables spoil quickly and travel poorly, so they are traded locally rather than across the whole nation.

options.text: world market
options.explanation: A world market suits goods traded across the globe; perishable vegetables are a local-market good.

questions.sourceRef: Area classification: perishable/bulky goods → local market

questions.stem: Market equilibrium price is the price at which:

options.text: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
options.explanation: Correct. At equilibrium the quantity buyers want to buy exactly equals the quantity sellers want to sell, so the market clears.

options.text: quantity demanded is greatest
options.explanation: Quantity demanded is greatest at the lowest price, not at equilibrium. Equilibrium balances the two quantities.

options.text: quantity supplied is greatest
options.explanation: Quantity supplied is greatest at the highest price, not at equilibrium.

options.text: the government fixes the price
options.explanation: Equilibrium is set by demand and supply, not by an administered price.

questions.sourceRef: Equilibrium: quantity demanded = quantity supplied

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Price determination · Surplus and shortage
questions.stem: When the market price is set ABOVE the equilibrium price, the result is:

options.text: a shortage, and price is bid up
options.explanation: A shortage arises below equilibrium, where demand exceeds supply. Above equilibrium the opposite happens.

options.text: a surplus, and price is pushed down toward equilibrium
options.explanation: Correct. Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded — a surplus — so sellers cut the price back toward equilibrium.

options.text: equilibrium is unaffected
options.explanation: A price away from equilibrium creates pressure. Above it there is excess supply, which moves the price.

options.text: both demand and supply become zero
options.explanation: Quantities do not fall to zero; supply simply exceeds demand, creating a surplus.

questions.sourceRef: Above equilibrium → surplus (excess supply) → price falls

questions.stem: In a market, Qd = 240 − 5P and Qs = 3P − 80, where P is the price in rupees. The equilibrium price is:

options.explanation: At ₹ 30, Qd = 240 − 150 = 90 and Qs = 90 − 80 = 10; the two are not equal, so ₹ 30 is not equilibrium.
Correct. Setting 240 − 5P = 3P − 80 gives 320 = 8P, so P = ₹ 40; then Qd = Qs = 40 units.
At ₹ 50, Qd = 240 − 250 = −10, which is impossible; the balancing price is ₹ 40.
At ₹ 20, Qd = 140 but Qs = −20; supply is not even positive here, so ₹ 20 is far from equilibrium.

questions.sourceRef: Solve Qd = Qs: 240 − 5P = 3P − 80 → P = 40

questions.stem: In a market, Qd = 120 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 60, where P is the price in rupees. The equilibrium quantity is:

options.text: 40 units
options.explanation: 40 is not the equilibrium quantity here. Solving gives P = ₹ 30 and quantity = 120 − 60 = 60 units.

options.text: 50 units
options.explanation: 50 does not satisfy both equations. At the equilibrium price ₹ 30 the quantity is 60 units.

options.text: 60 units
options.explanation: Correct. 120 − 2P = 4P − 60 gives 180 = 6P, so P = ₹ 30; then quantity = 120 − 2(30) = 60 units.

options.text: 30 units
options.explanation: 30 is the equilibrium price, not the quantity. Substituting P = 30 gives a quantity of 60 units.

questions.sourceRef: Solve Qd = Qs: P = 30, quantity = 120 − 2(30) = 60

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Price determination · Effect of demand shift
questions.stem: Other things equal, an INCREASE in demand (a rightward shift) will:

options.text: raise both the equilibrium price and quantity
options.explanation: Correct. A rightward demand shift moves along the supply curve, raising both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity.

options.text: lower both the equilibrium price and quantity
options.explanation: Both falling is the result of a decrease in demand, not an increase.

options.text: raise price but lower quantity
options.explanation: A demand shift moves price and quantity the same way; they do not move in opposite directions.

options.text: lower price but raise quantity
options.explanation: Price down with quantity up is the result of a supply increase, not a demand increase.

readLink.label: Read: Shifts in demand and supply, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Demand increase → price and quantity both rise

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Price determination · Effect of supply shift
questions.stem: Other things equal, an INCREASE in supply (a rightward shift) will:

options.text: raise price and lower quantity
options.explanation: Price up with quantity down is a supply decrease, not an increase.

options.text: lower the equilibrium price and raise the equilibrium quantity
options.explanation: Correct. A rightward supply shift moves along the demand curve, lowering the price and raising the quantity traded.

options.text: raise both price and quantity
options.explanation: Both rising is the result of a demand increase, not a supply increase.

options.text: leave price and quantity unchanged
options.explanation: A supply shift definitely moves the equilibrium; the price falls and the quantity rises.

readLink.label: Read: Shifts in demand and supply, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Supply increase → price falls, quantity rises

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Price determination · Demand vs supply shift pattern
questions.stem: Which statement about the direction of change is correct?

options.text: A demand shift moves price and quantity in the same direction; a supply shift moves them in opposite directions
options.explanation: Correct. A demand shift changes price and quantity together; a supply shift changes them oppositely (price one way, quantity the other).

options.text: Both a demand shift and a supply shift move price and quantity in the same direction
options.explanation: Only a demand shift moves them the same way; a supply shift moves them oppositely.

options.text: A demand shift moves them in opposite directions
options.explanation: This is reversed. A demand shift moves price and quantity in the same direction.

options.text: Neither shift changes the equilibrium
options.explanation: Both shifts change the equilibrium; the question is only about the direction of the change.

readLink.label: Read: Shifts in demand and supply, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Demand shift: same direction; supply shift: opposite directions

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Price determination · Equilibrium after a shift
questions.stem: A market has Qd = 200 − 4P and Qs = 6P − 100 (equilibrium price ₹ 30). Supply then rises so that Qs = 6P − 40. The new equilibrium price is:

options.explanation: ₹ 30 was the old equilibrium. After supply increases the price must fall, not stay the same.
Correct. 200 − 4P = 6P − 40 gives 240 = 10P, so P = ₹ 24 — lower than ₹ 30, as a supply increase requires.
At ₹ 20, Qd = 120 but the new Qs = 80; they are unequal, so ₹ 20 is not the new equilibrium.
At ₹ 26, Qd = 96 but the new Qs = 116; the balancing price is ₹ 24, not ₹ 26.

readLink.label: Read: Shifts in demand and supply, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Supply rises: 200 − 4P = 6P − 40 → P = 24 (down from 30)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Price determination · Both curves shift
questions.stem: If BOTH demand and supply increase at the same time, then with certainty:

options.text: the equilibrium quantity rises, but the price change is uncertain
options.explanation: Correct. Both increases push quantity up, so quantity certainly rises; the price could rise or fall depending on the relative sizes of the two shifts.

options.text: the equilibrium price rises, but the quantity change is uncertain
options.explanation: This is reversed. With both curves shifting right, quantity is the certain variable and price is the uncertain one.

options.text: both price and quantity rise
options.explanation: Price is not certain when both curves shift; it depends on which shift is larger. Only quantity is certain to rise.

options.text: both price and quantity fall
options.explanation: Quantity rises when both curves shift right; it does not fall. Price alone is ambiguous.

readLink.label: Read: Shifts in demand and supply, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Both curves shift right: quantity certainly rises, price ambiguous

questions.stem: Average revenue (AR) of a firm is equal to:

options.text: the price per unit of the good
options.explanation: Correct. AR = total revenue ÷ quantity = price, so the AR curve is the firm's demand curve.

options.text: total revenue minus total cost
options.explanation: That is profit, not average revenue. AR is revenue per unit, which equals price.

options.text: the change in total revenue from one more unit
options.explanation: That is marginal revenue, not average revenue. AR is revenue per unit sold.

options.text: total cost divided by output
options.explanation: That is average cost, not average revenue. AR uses revenue, not cost.

readLink.label: Read: Revenue — TR, AR and MR, §7 →

questions.sourceRef: AR = TR ÷ Q = price; AR curve is the demand curve

questions.stem: Marginal revenue (MR) is defined as:

options.text: total revenue divided by quantity sold
options.explanation: That is average revenue (price), not marginal revenue.

options.text: the addition to total revenue from selling one more unit
options.explanation: Correct. MR is the change in total revenue when output is increased by one unit: MR = TR(n) − TR(n − 1).

options.text: price multiplied by quantity
options.explanation: That is total revenue, not marginal revenue. MR is the increase in TR from one extra unit.

options.text: the price of the last unit only
options.explanation: The price of the last unit is its AR. MR is the change in total revenue, which differs from price when the demand curve slopes down.

readLink.label: Read: Revenue — TR, AR and MR, §7 →

questions.sourceRef: MR of nth unit = TR(n) − TR(n − 1)

questions.stem: A firm sells 20 units and earns a total revenue of ₹ 2,400. Its average revenue is:

options.explanation: Correct. AR = TR ÷ quantity = 2,400 ÷ 20 = ₹ 120, which is also the price per unit.
₹ 48 does not come from 2,400 ÷ 20. Average revenue is 2,400 ÷ 20 = ₹ 120.
₹ 2,400 is the total revenue, not the average. Divide by 20 units to get AR = ₹ 120.
2,400 ÷ 20 is ₹ 120, not ₹ 100. Recheck the division.

readLink.label: Read: Revenue — TR, AR and MR, §7 →

questions.stem: When a firm's output rises from 10 to 11 units, its total revenue rises from ₹ 500 to ₹ 540. The marginal revenue of the 11th unit is:

options.explanation: Correct. MR = change in TR = 540 − 500 = ₹ 40 for the 11th unit.
₹ 540 is the new total revenue, not the marginal revenue. MR is the change, 540 − 500 = ₹ 40.
₹ 500 is the old total revenue. Marginal revenue is the increase, ₹ 40.
₹ 49 (540 ÷ 11) is the new average revenue, not the marginal revenue. MR is 540 − 500 = ₹ 40.

readLink.label: Read: Revenue — TR, AR and MR, §7 →

questions.stem: When a firm's demand curve slopes downward, the relationship between AR and MR is that:

options.text: MR is equal to AR at every output
options.explanation: MR equals AR only when the demand curve is horizontal (perfect competition), not when it slopes down.

options.text: MR lies below AR, and MR falls faster than AR
options.explanation: Correct. Selling one more unit means cutting the price on all units, so the extra revenue is less than the price; MR lies below AR and falls faster.

options.text: MR lies above AR
options.explanation: MR never lies above AR on a downward-sloping demand curve; it lies below AR.

options.text: MR is always zero
options.explanation: MR is not always zero; it falls as output rises and reaches zero only where total revenue is at its maximum.

readLink.label: Read: Revenue — TR, AR and MR, §7 →

questions.sourceRef: Downward demand: MR below AR, MR falls faster; TR max where MR = 0

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Revenue · AR and MR under perfect competition
questions.stem: Under perfect competition, the relationship between price, AR and MR for the firm is:

options.text: price = AR = MR
options.explanation: Correct. The firm's demand curve is horizontal, so price does not change with output and price equals both average and marginal revenue.

options.text: price = AR, but MR is below AR
options.explanation: MR is below AR only when the demand curve slopes down. Under perfect competition the curve is horizontal, so MR = AR.

options.text: price is above AR
options.explanation: Price always equals AR by definition. It cannot be above it.

options.text: MR is above the price
options.explanation: MR equals the price under perfect competition; it is never above it.

questions.sourceRef: Perfect competition: P = AR = MR (horizontal demand)

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Revenue · MR under perfect competition
questions.stem: A perfectly competitive firm sells its output at the ruling market price of ₹ 25 per unit. Its marginal revenue is:

options.explanation: ₹ 12.50 (half the price) has no basis here. Under perfect competition MR equals the full price.
Correct. The firm is a price taker with a horizontal demand curve, so MR = AR = price = ₹ 25 for every unit.
MR is zero only where total revenue peaks on a downward demand curve. A price taker's MR equals the price, ₹ 25.
MR cannot exceed the price. Under perfect competition MR equals the price, ₹ 25.

questions.sourceRef: Price taker: MR = price = 25

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Equilibrium of the firm · Profit-max rule
questions.stem: A firm maximises its profit at the output where:

options.text: marginal revenue equals marginal cost, with MC rising
options.explanation: Correct. Profit is largest where MR = MC and marginal cost is rising through marginal revenue; beyond that point the next unit costs more than it earns.

options.text: total revenue equals total cost
options.explanation: TR = TC is the break-even (normal-profit) point, not the profit-maximising point. Profit is maximised where MR = MC.

options.text: average revenue equals average cost
options.explanation: AR = AC means normal profit (zero supernormal profit), not the profit-maximising condition.

options.text: marginal revenue is greatest
options.explanation: The firm expands only while MR exceeds MC, stopping where they are equal; the greatest MR is not the rule.

questions.sourceRef: Profit maximised where MR = MC, MC rising

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Equilibrium of the firm · Expand or contract
questions.stem: If, at its current output, a firm finds that marginal revenue is GREATER than marginal cost, it should:

options.text: increase output, because the extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost
options.explanation: Correct. While MR exceeds MC, each additional unit adds more to revenue than to cost, so expanding output raises profit until MR = MC.

options.text: reduce output at once
options.explanation: Reducing output is right only when MC exceeds MR. Here MR is above MC, so expansion raises profit.

options.text: keep output unchanged, since profit is already maximised
options.explanation: Profit is maximised only where MR = MC. With MR above MC there is still profit to gain by expanding.

options.text: shut down immediately
options.explanation: Shutdown relates to price falling below average variable cost, not to MR exceeding MC. Here the firm should expand.

questions.sourceRef: MR > MC → expand output to raise profit

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Equilibrium of the firm · MR = MC output
questions.stem: A firm's marginal cost for successive units is ₹ 12, ₹ 14, ₹ 16, ₹ 18 and ₹ 20, and its marginal revenue is constant at ₹ 16. The profit-maximising output is:

options.text: 2 units
options.explanation: At 2 units MC is ₹ 14, still below MR ₹ 16, so the firm can profitably produce the 3rd unit too.

options.text: 3 units
options.explanation: Correct. The firm produces every unit whose MC does not exceed MR ₹ 16: units 1, 2 and 3 (MC ₹ 12, 14, 16). The 4th unit's MC ₹ 18 exceeds MR, so output is 3 units, where MR = MC = ₹ 16.

options.text: 4 units
options.explanation: The 4th unit costs ₹ 18, above MR ₹ 16, so it would reduce profit. Output stops at 3 units.

options.text: 5 units
options.explanation: The 4th and 5th units both cost more than MR ₹ 16, so producing them cuts profit. Output is 3 units.

questions.sourceRef: Produce units with MC ≤ MR 16: units 1–3; output = 3

questions.stem: A monopolist sets a price of ₹ 50 per unit and sells 12 units. Its total revenue is:

options.explanation: Correct. TR = price × quantity = 50 × 12 = ₹ 600.
₹ 62 is 50 + 12, an addition. Total revenue multiplies price by quantity: 50 × 12 = ₹ 600.
₹ 50 is the price per unit, not total revenue. Multiply by the 12 units to get ₹ 600.
50 × 12 is ₹ 600, not ₹ 500. Recheck the multiplication.

readLink.label: Read: Revenue — TR, AR and MR, §7 →

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Equilibrium of the firm · Profit calculation
questions.stem: At its profit-maximising output a firm's total revenue is ₹ 9,000 and its total cost is ₹ 7,200. Its profit is:

options.explanation: Correct. Profit = TR − TC = 9,000 − 7,200 = ₹ 1,800.
₹ 16,200 adds TR and TC. Profit subtracts cost from revenue: 9,000 − 7,200 = ₹ 1,800.
₹ 7,200 is the total cost, not the profit. Profit is 9,000 − 7,200 = ₹ 1,800.
₹ 9,000 is total revenue, not profit. Profit is TR − TC = ₹ 1,800.

questions.stem: A firm under perfect competition is called a 'price taker' because:

options.text: it must accept the price set by the industry's demand and supply
options.explanation: Correct. Each firm is too small to affect the market price, so it accepts (takes) the ruling price and can sell any quantity at it.

options.text: it sets the price to maximise its profit
options.explanation: Setting the price describes a price maker (monopoly), not a price taker in perfect competition.

options.text: it charges different prices to different buyers
options.explanation: Charging different prices is price discrimination, possible under monopoly, not in perfect competition where one price rules.

options.text: it faces a downward-sloping demand curve
options.explanation: A price taker faces a horizontal demand curve. A downward-sloping firm demand curve belongs to the price-making forms.

questions.sourceRef: Perfect competition firm is a price taker (horizontal demand)

questions.stem: In the SHORT RUN, a perfectly competitive firm earns supernormal profit when:

options.text: price (AR) is greater than average cost
options.explanation: Correct. When price exceeds average cost, total revenue exceeds total cost, so the firm earns supernormal profit in the short run.

options.text: price equals average cost
options.explanation: Price equal to average cost gives only normal profit, not supernormal profit.

options.text: price is below average cost
options.explanation: Price below average cost gives a loss, not a supernormal profit.

options.text: price equals marginal revenue
options.explanation: Price always equals MR under perfect competition; this alone says nothing about profit, which depends on AR versus AC.

questions.sourceRef: Short run: AR > AC → supernormal profit

questions.stem: In LONG-RUN equilibrium under perfect competition, each firm earns:

options.text: supernormal profit, because entry is blocked
options.explanation: Entry is free under perfect competition, so supernormal profit cannot persist; it is competed away.

options.text: only normal profit, with price equal to the minimum of average cost
options.explanation: Correct. Free entry and exit drive the price to the minimum of long-run average cost, where P = AR = MR = MC = minimum AC and only normal profit remains.

options.text: a permanent loss
options.explanation: A firm making a loss would leave in the long run, raising the price; the long-run outcome is normal profit, not a loss.

options.text: normal profit but with excess capacity
options.explanation: Excess capacity is the long-run result of monopolistic competition. Under perfect competition the firm sits at minimum AC with no excess capacity.

questions.sourceRef: Long run: P = minimum LAC, only normal profit, no excess capacity

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Equilibrium of the firm · Profit from AC and price
questions.stem: A firm produces 50 units, its average cost is ₹ 18 per unit, and it sells each unit at ₹ 24. Its total profit is:

options.explanation: Correct. Profit per unit = price − average cost = 24 − 18 = ₹ 6; total profit = 6 × 50 = ₹ 300.
₹ 1,200 is total revenue (24 × 50), not profit. Subtract total cost (18 × 50 = ₹ 900) to get profit ₹ 300.
₹ 900 is total cost (18 × 50), not profit. Profit is 1,200 − 900 = ₹ 300.
₹ 6 is the profit per unit, not the total. Multiply by 50 units to get ₹ 300.

questions.stem: A monopolist is described as a 'price maker' because:

options.text: it can set the price, choosing a point on the market demand curve
options.explanation: Correct. As the only seller, the monopolist can set the price, but only along the demand curve — a higher price still means fewer units sold.

options.text: it can sell any quantity at a fixed price set by others
options.explanation: That describes a price taker under perfect competition, not a monopolist.

options.text: it faces a horizontal demand curve
options.explanation: A horizontal demand curve belongs to the price taker. The monopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand curve.

options.text: its price is fixed by the industry supply curve
options.explanation: The monopolist is the whole industry; there is no separate industry price to accept. It sets its own price.

questions.sourceRef: Monopolist is a price maker along the demand curve

questions.stem: At the monopolist's profit-maximising output (where MR = MC), the price charged is:

options.text: equal to marginal revenue
options.explanation: Price equals MR only under perfect competition. For a monopolist, price is read off the higher AR curve and exceeds MR.

options.text: greater than marginal revenue and marginal cost
options.explanation: Correct. The monopolist equates MR and MC, then charges the price on the AR (demand) curve above that output, so price is greater than MR = MC.

options.text: below marginal cost
options.explanation: The monopolist would not price below marginal cost; the price on the demand curve lies above MR = MC.

options.text: equal to average cost always
options.explanation: Price equals average cost only in the special case of normal profit. In general the monopolist's price exceeds MR = MC and can leave supernormal profit.

questions.sourceRef: Monopoly: equilibrium at MR = MC, price from AR, so P > MR = MC

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Monopoly · MR from AR schedule
questions.stem: A monopolist can sell 5 units at a price of ₹ 20 each and 6 units at a price of ₹ 18 each. The marginal revenue of the 6th unit is:

options.explanation: ₹ 18 is the price (AR) of the 6th unit, not its marginal revenue. Because the price falls on all units, MR is lower than the price.
Correct. TR at 5 units = 20 × 5 = ₹ 100; TR at 6 units = 18 × 6 = ₹ 108; MR = 108 − 100 = ₹ 8, well below the price of ₹ 18.
₹ 2 is the ₹ 20 − ₹ 18 fall in price, not the marginal revenue. MR is the change in total revenue, ₹ 8.
₹ 108 is the new total revenue, not the marginal revenue. MR is the change, 108 − 100 = ₹ 8.

questions.sourceRef: TR: 100 → 108; MR of 6th unit = 8 (below AR 18)

questions.stem: Unlike a perfectly competitive firm, a monopolist can earn supernormal profit even in the long run because:

options.text: entry of new firms is blocked, so profit is not competed away
options.explanation: Correct. Barriers to entry keep out new firms, so the supernormal profit that free entry would erode under competition can persist for the monopolist.

options.text: the monopolist always faces a horizontal demand curve
options.explanation: The monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, not a horizontal one; blocked entry, not the curve's shape, protects its profit.

options.text: its marginal revenue equals its price
options.explanation: MR is below price for a monopolist. What sustains long-run profit is blocked entry, not any MR = price relation.

options.text: it must sell at the minimum of average cost
options.explanation: Selling at minimum average cost is the competitive long-run result giving only normal profit. Blocked entry lets the monopolist do better.

questions.sourceRef: Monopoly long-run supernormal profit persists due to blocked entry

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a condition necessary for price discrimination by a monopolist?

options.text: The seller has monopoly power over the price
options.explanation: This is a required condition: only a price maker can charge different prices for the same good.

options.text: The markets can be kept separate so the good cannot be resold
options.explanation: This is a required condition: if buyers could resell from the cheap to the dear market, the price gap would collapse.

options.text: The two markets have different elasticities of demand
options.explanation: This is a required condition: different elasticities are what make it profitable to charge different prices.

options.text: The product must be identical across all sellers in the market
options.explanation: Correct. This is NOT a condition; price discrimination is a single seller's practice, so a homogeneous product across many sellers is irrelevant to it.

questions.sourceRef: Discrimination conditions: monopoly power, separable markets, different elasticities

questions.topic: Ch 4 · Monopoly · Degrees of price discrimination
questions.stem: Charging a different price in each SEPARATE market or group of buyers (for example, student versus regular fares) is an example of:

options.text: first-degree (perfect) price discrimination
options.explanation: First-degree discrimination charges a different price for every single unit, taking the whole consumer surplus, not a group price.

options.text: second-degree price discrimination
options.explanation: Second-degree discrimination charges different prices for different blocks of quantity (slab tariffs), not different groups of buyers.

options.text: third-degree price discrimination
options.explanation: Correct. Third-degree discrimination charges a different price in each separate market or group of buyers, the most common form.

options.text: no price discrimination at all
options.explanation: Charging groups different prices for the same good is discrimination; specifically it is the third degree.

questions.sourceRef: Third-degree discrimination: different price per separate market/group

questions.stem: A monopolist's total revenue is ₹ 240 when it sells 10 units and ₹ 231 when it sells 11 units. The marginal revenue of the 11th unit is:

options.explanation: The sign is wrong. Total revenue fell from ₹ 240 to ₹ 231, so the marginal revenue is negative, −₹ 9, not +₹ 9.
Correct. MR = change in TR = 231 − 240 = −₹ 9. Beyond the revenue-maximising output MR turns negative, because the price cut on all units outweighs the extra unit sold.
₹ 21 (231 ÷ 11) is close to the new average revenue, not the marginal revenue. MR is the change in total revenue, −₹ 9.
MR would be zero only if total revenue were unchanged. Here TR fell by ₹ 9, so MR = −₹ 9.

questions.sourceRef: MR = 231 − 240 = −9 (negative beyond TR maximum)

questions.stem: The expenditure a firm incurs on advertising and salesmanship to promote its differentiated product is called:

options.text: selling cost
options.explanation: Correct. Selling costs are outlays on advertising and salesmanship to shift and steepen the firm's demand curve — a feature of monopolistic competition, absent under perfect competition.

options.text: marginal cost
options.explanation: Marginal cost is the addition to total production cost from one more unit, not the cost of promotion.

options.text: fixed cost of plant
options.explanation: Fixed cost is the cost of the fixed factors like plant and machinery, not the cost of advertising.

options.text: opportunity cost
options.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, a different concept from promotion outlays.

questions.sourceRef: Selling costs: advertising/salesmanship under monopolistic competition

questions.stem: In LONG-RUN equilibrium under monopolistic competition, a typical firm:

options.text: earns only normal profit and operates with excess capacity
options.explanation: Correct. Free entry competes away supernormal profit, so only normal profit remains; because demand slopes down, its tangency with average cost is to the left of minimum AC, leaving excess (unused) capacity.

options.text: earns supernormal profit protected by blocked entry
options.explanation: Entry is free under monopolistic competition, so supernormal profit is competed away; blocked entry belongs to monopoly.

options.text: produces at the minimum of average cost, like perfect competition
options.explanation: It does not reach minimum average cost. The downward-sloping demand curve is tangent to AC to the left of its minimum, giving excess capacity.

options.text: makes a permanent loss and shuts down
options.explanation: Firms making losses would leave, so the long-run outcome is normal profit, not a permanent loss.

questions.sourceRef: Monopolistic competition long run: normal profit + excess capacity

questions.stem: The demand curve faced by a firm under monopolistic competition is:

options.text: horizontal (perfectly elastic)
options.explanation: A horizontal demand curve belongs to perfect competition. Under monopolistic competition the product is differentiated, so the curve slopes down.

options.text: downward-sloping but highly elastic, because of close substitutes
options.explanation: Correct. Product differentiation gives the firm a downward-sloping demand curve, but the many close substitutes make it highly elastic.

options.text: vertical (perfectly inelastic)
options.explanation: A vertical demand curve would mean buyers never change quantity with price, which does not describe a market with close substitutes.

options.text: upward-sloping
options.explanation: Demand curves for these firms slope downward, not upward; more is bought at a lower price.

questions.sourceRef: Monopolistic competition: downward but highly elastic firm demand curve

questions.stem: The most important feature that distinguishes oligopoly from other market forms is:

options.text: interdependence of the firms' decisions
options.explanation: Correct. With only a few sellers, each firm's price and output decision affects the others, so every firm must anticipate its rivals' reactions — the defining feature of oligopoly.

options.text: a completely homogeneous product in every case
options.explanation: Oligopoly products may be identical or differentiated; the defining feature is interdependence, not homogeneity.

options.text: free and easy entry of new firms
options.explanation: Oligopoly usually has barriers to entry. Free entry describes the competitive forms.

options.text: a single seller of the product
options.explanation: A single seller is monopoly. Oligopoly has a few sellers who are interdependent.

questions.sourceRef: Oligopoly defining feature: interdependence of firms

questions.stem: The kinked demand curve model of oligopoly explains why:

options.text: prices tend to be rigid (sticky), changing less often than costs or demand would suggest
options.explanation: Correct. Rivals match price cuts but not price rises, so demand is elastic above and inelastic below the ruling price; the gap in MR at the kink keeps the profit-maximising price unchanged despite small cost changes.

options.text: prices change constantly with every cost movement
options.explanation: The model explains the opposite — price rigidity. The gap in MR means small cost changes leave the price unchanged.

options.text: the firm always earns only normal profit
options.explanation: The kinked demand model is about price rigidity, not about the level of long-run profit.

options.text: entry into the industry is always free
options.explanation: The model is about pricing behaviour, not entry. Oligopoly typically has barriers to entry.

questions.sourceRef: Kinked demand: elastic above, inelastic below; MR gap → price rigidity

questions.stem: A formal agreement among a few sellers to fix the price and share the market between them is called a:

options.text: cartel
options.explanation: Correct. A cartel is a formal collusive agreement among oligopolists to fix price and share the market, acting like a single monopoly (OPEC is the classic example).

options.text: monopsony
options.explanation: A monopsony is a market with a single buyer, not a sellers' agreement.

options.text: perfectly competitive market
options.explanation: Perfect competition has many independent sellers and no agreement on price; a cartel is the opposite of that.

options.text: price-taking arrangement
options.explanation: Cartel members set (fix) the price together; they are price makers acting jointly, not price takers.

questions.sourceRef: Cartel: formal collusive agreement to fix price and share market
